Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Expectation2: Fix bugs and troubleshoot issues reported by users or QA
Situation2: A production outage traces back to a defect in their code and customers cannot access the service
Story: My phone buzzed with a message from Jamie: “Ugh, today was endless. Can I vent for a bit?” I glanced at the clock—6:13 p.m.—and my laptop screen, where error logs scrolled in red. The production outage was my fault; a bug I’d missed had brought the service down, and users were locked out. My team’s Slack was blowing up with urgent pings: “Can you look at this now?” “Any update?” My stomach twisted. Jamie needed me to listen, to be present, to offer the kind of support I always promised. But my team needed me to fix this, fast. I could almost hear the customers’ frustration echoing through the support tickets. My fingers hovered over my phone, torn between typing a comforting reply and diving back into the code. The weight of both expectations pressed on me, and I felt myself pulled in two directions, unable to give either the attention they deserved.
